Twenty Fourth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2003-2005
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 22, pp 239-246
Lake Bottom Sediment Coring from Schirmacher
Oasis During 24th Indian Antarctic Expedition
Rajesh Asthana, Prakash K. Shrivastava and K. Ramar
Geological Survey of India
 ABSTRACT
Lake sediment cores retrieved from pristine environment of Antarctica can
provide a high resolution palaeoclimatic record having a significant bearing on the
global climate change. The sedimentary layers at the lake bottom contain
chronologically ordered information. Studies on long term climatic changes in
Antarctica have been focused on ice core and marine records which have provided
insights about atmospheric / marine couplings during last glacial / interglacial cycle.
Owing to the lack of large ice-free areas and the presence of permafrost, terrestrial
records have played a less significant role in documenting Holocene climatic changes.
The Schirmacher Oasis is interspersed with a number of freshwater lakes
offering a great potential of systematic multi-disciplinary studies. The expertise of
retrieving in-situ lake bottom sediment cores using indigenously designed and
developed coring devise by Antarctica Division has yielded significant results.
Thus, a systematic attempt of Lake Bottom Sediment Coring was made during the
24
th Indian Antarctic Expedition mainly during the wintering over period.
INTRODUCTION
Limnological studies from Antarctic Peninsula, McMurdo Dry Valley
and East Antarctic lake-rich Oases: Vestfold Hills, Larsemann Hills, Bunger
Hills, Rauer Islands and Windmill Islands have already contributed
significantly in the various aspects of lacustrine systems. Earlier attempts
of retrieving Lake Bottom sediment cores from Schirmacher Oasis
succeeded in getting a few cores of about 50 to 70 cm lengths. Studies on
these cores led to an inference indicating a three fold climatic oscillation
(warm-dry, warm-humid and warm more humid) since last 8,000 BP (Bera
and Khandelwal, 2003; Bera, 2004; Bera, 2006) besides identification of
the first record of some Arcellaceans (Mathur et al., 2006) which are very
important ecological indicators.
240 Rajesh Asthana et al.
Allowing the scope of expansion and improvement of scientific
information based on lake bottom sediment cores, a total number of 39
lake bottom sediment cores (cumulative core length - 43.50m) have been
retrieved using indigenously designed and fabricated sediment coring device
during the austral winter of 24
th Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica
(2004 – 06). From each coring site, entire sedimentation column from top
to bedrock have been raised with some cores of more than 200 cm lengths
(longest core being 221 cm) that are likely to provide data beyond LGM. A
comprehensive multidisciplinary investigation including sedimentological,
geochemical, biological, palynological, micropalaeontological and mineral
magnetic susceptibility studies have been envisaged (Asthana et al., 2006)
along with isotopic and thermo luminescence (TL) dating to elucidate
various parameters. Synthesis of all these data would be helpful in
reconstructing the palaeoclimatic and palaeoenvironmental regimes of East
Antarctica that will have a bearing on the global climatic changes in recent
geologic past.
Lacustrine Environment at Schirmacher Oasis, Sediment
Characteristics and Scope of Investigation
The “roche moutonnee” landscape of Schirmacher Oasis is
characterized by numerous lakes which are mostly ice-scoured basins and
troughs (Beg et al., 2006) produced by moving ice streams/ice sheets
subsequent to the Last Glacial Maximum. Sediments derived from the ice
masses are transported and deposited by melt water and these sedimentary
layers at the lake bottom contain chronologically ordered information
regarding the topography and environmental history of the region.
The glacial and periglacial environments encompassing lakes of
varying dimensions are characterized by specific physical, chemical and
biological conditions and the major glacial activities involve both erosion
and sedimentation. Lacustrine systems are very sensitive and readily affected
by even minor tectonic or climatic changes, interacting tectonics, drainage
evolution and sediment supply that get preserved in their depositional
records.
All major lakes of Schirmacher Oasis are localized along the glacial
valleys (Ravindra et al., 2002; Beg et al., 2006). The older (first generation)
valleys are separated by high grounds with typical development of Roche
Moutonnees; whereas steep and clean cut walls define the younger ones.
